Roman dream of building structure over strait of Messina has been revived by officials, despite claims it is unworkable and protests from locals

For more than 2,000 years, it has been an obsessive dream: a plan to link the Mediterranean Sea’s largest island to mainland Italy. It began with the Romans, who, according to Pliny the Elder, built a bridge of boats and barrels across the strait of Messina in 251BC to transport 140 war elephants captured from the Carthaginians.

Centuries later, the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini embraced the same vision, followed by rightwing prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who made the bridge a flagship project. Then, in 2022, after being appointed Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini revived the mythic ambition, claiming that the ferry crossings “cost people more in a year than it would cost to build the bridge”.

item.title: Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
It’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimistic

Here in Silicon Valley, the experts think that within the next couple of years we’ll see an extraordinary takeoff for artificial intelligence. “Welcome to the foothills of the singularity,” as a Stanford University friend greeted me. More prosaically, the imminent breakthrough is described as “recursive self-improvement” – the point at which AI itself trains each successive model of AI, resulting in an exponential development to something which, in many significant respects, is more intelligent than us humans.

As Robert Wright puts it in his book The God Test: “Never before has the near-term future … held such a wide array of not-implausible paths for humankind that would be so wildly transformative.” But will this be heaven or hell? Heaven, says Elon Musk, who predicts “an age of amazing abundance” – although he also sees a 10-20% chance of killer robots murdering us all. Hell is more likely according to Geoffrey Hinton, one of the intellectual founding fathers of AI. “My intuition is, we’re toast,” he told an interviewer in 2023. And talking to Sebastian Mallaby, author of The Infinity Machine, a book about the quest for superintelligence, Hinton estimates p(doom) – the probability of human extinction – at 50%, “because I haven’t got a clue how to estimate the real number”. “As soon as evolution [of AI] kicks in, we’re fucked,” he adds cheerfully. But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.

Timothy Garton Ash is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights | Moira Donegan
item.description:
A call revealing Todd Blanche’s plans to crack down on mifepristone lays bare the danger

The abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it.

So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally when Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general.

item.title: AI has young writers between a rock and a hard place
item.description:
Buzzwords, clichéd phrases, formulaic sentences, and most notoriously—the use of the em dash. These are all signs readers and writers alike have learned to look out for when trying to spot whether something was written by AI. 

Authors and journalists have faced the brunt of this trend, with accusations of AI use increasing as AI becomes more normalized. Tools can sniff out artificial intelligence, but they can be imperfect and unreliable. 

Between discouraging allegations and increased scrutiny over common writing practices, young writers are beginning to lose motivation, even as their level of AI adoption may vary. According to the Society of Authors, 20% of fiction writers and 25% of nonfiction writers stated that they use AI. But 65% of fiction writers and 57% of nonfiction writers believe AI will hurt their future income from their creative work. 

Alex Del Cueto, a recent college graduate who is an arts journalist at Broadway World, a theatre news website, says he’s concerned about entering the workforce during the rise of AI. “I feel like the rise of AI and its effects [have] made being a young journalist almost impossible,” he says. The growing use of the technology has complicated an already difficult job market in an already competitive field.  

Thanks to AI, young writers are left in limbo. They’re simultaneously struggling to figure out if they need to use AI to keep up in today’s competitive industry—or eschew it altogether in order to maintain trust. (Em dashes and all.)

AI can damage reputation—and mental health

Amid prompts to chatbots being left behind in published books and AI creating fake quotes used in articles, distrust has grown between the audience and writers. In this new world where readers don’t know who (or what) is doing the writing, anything can set off alarm bells for the audience: a new word, offbeat punctuation, or even the content itself. 

People have taken to calling anything they don’t like AI. Whether it’s a book, a photo or video, or an article, “that’s AI” is being used as an insult rather than a legitimate accusation. This can lead to harassment of the creator and a deleterious domino effect on creatives. 

Writers who have been falsely accused of using AI in their writing, for example, have voiced anxiety and disappointment when they come across the negative review. Instead of critiquing nuanced parts of the writing, commenters just throw out the accusation and call it a day. 

In addition to being bad for their mental health, this trend can be extremely harmful to people’s careers. Younger writers have voiced fears of losing a job they don’t even have yet to AI. 

Some writers are now shying away from using language and punctuation that has become associated with AI, like saying something is “X, not Y,” an LLM go-to. For instance: “Using AI isn’t cheating. It’s leveraging resources.”

So instead of developing the fundamentals of their craft, writers can be left focusing on whether their work sounds like it could be written by a bot. “What if I use the em dash too much?” or “Will people believe that I really organically use that word?” start taking over. 

Barb Kay, a student at Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York, says using AI can be a stigma for writers. And seeing it used in methods of research, or to help write a story, can feel discouraging for the writers themselves. 

“I feel discouraged by the implementation of AI in the newsroom and am skeptical of my colleagues who use it,” she says. “While I try to keep an open mind, the harm it does to the environment, and the risk of losing human connection and journalistic integrity, outweigh any benefit it might have.” 

And yet, some writers may still use it 

Despite the stigma and risks, AI is here to stay—and many professionals, including writers, may use it for a variety of purposes. That decision isn’t always born out of laziness or lack of creativity. Sometimes it’s a last resort. 

Some authors who have been accused of AI have admitted to using it to edit their work due to busy schedules, balancing parenting and other jobs, or important responsibilities. Others work independently, and don’t have the budget to pay a real editor to look over their work. 

This isn’t only an individual issue, but a media issue; as the United Nations communications department points out, traditional media outlets are under financial strain. Newsrooms with smaller staffs under pressure to meet traffic targets may prioritize output over quality. 

Creative fields are already hard to break into. So some writers feel the need to take matters into their own hands. 

Platforms like River AI, where writers can use AI to edit and proofread big projects like books, have become more popular. As a result, the number of self-published books has increased for fictional titles in recent years. 

Where does this leave young writers? 

Freelancers or authors with no publishing deal to rely on may be short on money, putting them under intense competitive pressure in a competitive industry. Those who are anti-AI may feel a pull towards using it to vie for an audience, produce material quickly, or gain traffic. 

Another graduate student journalist at Craig Newmark, Natalie Tulloch, says she’s seen newsrooms, both academically and professionally, suggest using AI to take on research tasks. And she wonders why. She feels confident that the research AI can conduct, a human could do better. 

“I think it’s a scary thing, but the more I get [close] to entering the workforce, the more it makes me want to be even better, to prove that AI can’t replace me,” she says.

The human condition of writing

The rise of AI will continue to affect up-and-coming writers. 

Although younger generations report higher levels of skepticism when it comes to the harm AI may cause, the number of young adults using AI keeps increasing. Some media outlets and publishers have tried to combat growing misinformation and alert readers when AI has had a hand in work. 

In March 2026, the Authors Guild allowed authors to add an official certification (the “Human Authored Certification”) to their books in the United States. This would be proof that a book was entirely written by a human, and that minimal to no AI writing tools were used for assistance. Since this option arrived, thousands of authors have employed it in an attempt to distance themselves as much as possible from potential accusations. 

Belle Martinelli, who works as a member services coordinator at the Greater Olean Area Chamber of Commerce in New York while freelancing as a journalist, says the people around her “treat me like an alien” when she tells them she doesn’t use AI. 

“I’m a writer. I love to write,” she says. “I go out, and I report, and I come back and I write. If you can’t do that without a robot you have no business being a journalist . . . because journalism is more than just pen-on-paper writing. It’s about telling stories, telling information, but it’s about moving people. You can’t move people as a robot.” 

When we use AI for creative work that a human can do, we risk undermining the editing process. If human decisions are replaced by AI, the writing will feel more disconnected. The way a writer connects with their audience is crucially human. Only a person can tell another person’s story, fictional or factual, in a way others can relate to and understand. 

That’s simply not something technology can replace.

item.description:
The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should

A fortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C. We stayed at a youth hostel – more of which in a moment – and began the trip with the 20-minute ascent of Mam Tor, a modest peak that pulls in both dedicated ramblers who then yomp along the ridge beyond, and newbies who mostly want to get to the top and immerse themselves in the jaw-dropping view.

The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

item.title: When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised | Sanghmitra Singh
item.description:
The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness

Scottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.

As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.

Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writer

item.title: Nuclear power is China’s key for transitioning to a fully renewable grid design
item.description:
Between late 2016 and August 2026, China connected 27 new nuclear reactors to its grid. In the same period, the United States connected two. As Jacopo Buongiorno—professor of nuclear science and engineering and director of the Center for Advanced Nuclear Energy Systems at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology—tells me, “China is the world’s leader in nuclear power plant (NPP) construction.”

It’s an impressive data point on its own but when you consider the greater picture, it’s even more striking. Those nuclear power plants are only a small fraction of China’s current power throughput, but they are the crux of the country’s electricity generation. The reason is that Chinese engineers have designed a power grid that relies heavily on renewables (and aims to eventually be 100% green). But, since wind and solar generation fluctuate a lot, they need a lot of nuclear generation to keep their electrical network stable and fully operational. Without that constant power, the fluctuations will make the grid crash.

Beijing’s electricity hunger traces back to Deng Xiaoping’s “Reform and Opening-Up” policies, launched in December 1978, which set China on a path of rapid industrialization, market liberalization, and urbanization that has continued for nearly five decades. That transformation drove a surge in electrification, originally fed by coal and, in recent years, increasingly by renewable energy.

“We’re in this incredible race to add enough power generation capacity in China to meet what is adding one extra Germany of new electricity consumption every year,” David Fishman, a principal at energy consultancy firm The Lantau Group, recently told the South China Morning Post.

The math checks out: China’s power consumption surpassed 10 trillion kilowatt-hours—10,000 terawatt-hours (TWh)—in 2025, pushed up by advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence. China’s electricity demand grew by 503 TWh that year alone. Germany’s gross electricity consumption, from every source combined, was estimated at roughly 517 TWh over the same period—meaning China added nearly one Germany’s worth of new demand in a single year.

Almost none of that growth is being met with nuclear power. Coal still supplies the largest share of China’s electricity, but renewables are closing the gap fast: Wind and solar rose to 22% of national generation in 2025, up from 18% the year before, and by the first half of 2026, coal’s share had fallen below 50% of total generation for the first time on record. Nuclear, meanwhile, holds steady at about 5% of the mix.

If the extreme electricity build-up is almost entirely driven by wind and solar now, why is nuclear so important for China’s power grid design? Designing a grid is not a matter of building power plants and connecting them to cities and factories the same way you connect your toaster to the wall plug. Energy production fluctuates, and every node in a national grid needs to be controlled and balanced so the entire network doesn’t go down (see what happened during the Spanish power outage last year, where renewables produce most of the energy now, but it’s not well balanced).

To avoid a disastrous Spanish situation, China has been doing two things for close to two decades now. First, building a “bullet train for power”—the world’s most extensive ultra-high-voltage grid, which carries electricity from wind and solar farms in the west to industrial hubs on the coast, balancing supply and demand across the country in real time. Second, building out a nuclear fleet that supplies power regardless of weather, wind speed, or time of day. That’s where nuclear energy comes in.

The atomic key

Nuclear supplies something called continuous baseload output to the power grid. A grid built overwhelmingly on intermittent generation needs a fixed floor under it, and nuclear is the floor Beijing has chosen in its race to zero-carbon power.

China currently operates 64 commercial reactors producing 63.9 gigawatts, the second-largest fleet in the world behind the U.S. Domestic companies are building 37 more units totaling 38.5 gigawatts. The State Council has approved 10 or more reactors annually since 2022, including eight units across four projects greenlit on July 31, 2026, worth $25 billion, on the way to 110 gigawatts of installed nuclear capacity by 2030 and a power mix that is 50% non-fossil.

The astonishing nuclear reactor construction speed comes first from standardization. China builds two pressurized water reactor designs almost exclusively: the domestic third-generation Hualong One, and the CAP1000, adapted from an American design created by Westinghouse.

“The supply chain is all built around this standardization,” Victor Nian of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources told the South China Morning Post. Domestic suppliers now manufacture nearly every component a new reactor needs. That repetition compresses build time to about five years per unit, while in the West we spend a decade or more.

You may think that, perhaps, China is skipping safety steps, but the fact is that they are not, Buongiorno tells me. The country’s existing fleet, essentially all water-cooled reactors, already operates safely and reliably, he says, and, “there is no reason to believe the NPPs being built now, which are essentially identical, will perform any differently.” He says that China, like every country that operates nuclear power plants, belongs to the World Association of Nuclear Operators, which conducts periodic reviews and inspections of member fleets. “China does not run these NPPs in isolation,” he points out.

The other element behind this speed is state financing, which compresses the cost curve the same way standardization compresses the timeline. According to the SCMP, developers borrow at interest rates as low as 1.5%, bringing the levelized cost of electricity for a 1-gigawatt reactor to roughly $42 per megawatt-hour, about half what a comparably financed Western project would cost.

Buongiorno frames this as a proven approach rather than an improvised one. “State-backed financing and stable energy policies are a good way to ensure these capital-intensive and long-duration projects can be carried out to completion with minimal perturbations,” he says, pointing to France’s nuclear build-out in the 1970s and 80s, and to India, Russia and South Korea today, as prior examples of the same model.

Beijing’s model has one major physical limit: China permits commercial reactors only on the coast, where suitable sites cap out at roughly 163 reactors. Beijing suspended approvals for inland reactors after the 2011 Fukushima meltdown. “China will physically run out of suitable sites at some point,” Fishman told the SCMP. Lifting that moratorium would open 77 sites nationwide with room for 345 reactors.

Buongiorno does not see the inland shift as a new category of risk, however. “Inland reactors are in operation in dozens of countries around the world,” he tells me. “Their risk profile depends on the specifics of the site—seismicity, water access, population density, etc. Nothing new here.”

item.title: The art of asking questions in a world full of answers
item.description:
Below, Lani Watson shares five key insights from her new book, Q: The Hidden Power of Questions in a World That Wants Answers.

Watson is a philosopher and Honorary Fellow at the University of Edinburgh. She is a world-leading expert in the philosophy of questions, having researched the topic for nearly two decades. Businesses and organizations around the world have sought her help in learning how to ask great questions.

What’s the Big Idea?

We’re living through uncertain, unsettling times, and every instinct pulls us toward quick, comforting answers. But certainty, chased too hard, makes us rigid and closed. Uncertainty isn’t a problem to be eliminated; it’s the texture of a rich, complicated, unpredictable life. Questioning is what lets us meet it, not with anxiety, but with openness, curiosity, and a little humility.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Watson herself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book.

1. Questions direct our attention.

I’ll start by asking you a question: Where are you? Take a moment with this.

It’s a very simple question, but notice that before you even answer, it has already had an effect. Perhaps you glanced unconsciously at your surroundings or thought briefly about the view in front of you or reflected on the journey you’re on. That’s the first hidden power of questions. They direct our attention instantly.

Nobody understands this better than magicians. Watch a close-up magic show and you’ll notice the magician asking questions: “What’s your name?” “Is this your first magic show?” “Can you check that this is a normal pack of cards?”

These questions are an integral part of the trick. Each one draws your attention to where the magician wants it, at precisely the moment the sleight of hand happens somewhere else.

Psychologists have even tested this in the lab: Volunteers are told to watch a simple card trick and not be distracted. Yet the moment the magician asks a question, almost everyone instinctively looks up at their face; the move is made right under their nose, and most people don’t even remember looking away.

That’s how strong the attentional pull of a question is. Even when we’re actively trying to resist it, we can’t. This is why I describe questioning as an attentional mechanism. Questions influence what we notice and what we miss. And because attention shapes what we think, how we feel, and what we do, the questions running through your day are quietly steering your life.

Magicians use this attentional effect to surprise and delight us, but the same force is at work everywhere, all the time. The questions a doctor asks determine the diagnosis you get. The questions you ask at work affect how others see you. The question a headline asks influences what you click. Change the question, and you change the direction of travel.

The trouble is that questions are so familiar we barely notice them. We rush past the question to grab the answer, but by then the question has already chosen where we’re going. If you want to understand your experiences, relationships, work, or the world around you, start by noticing the questions quietly moving your attention.

2. Questions change our brains.

The power of questions begins in your head. Think of a question that has genuinely gripped you: a half-remembered piece of trivia that you couldn’t quite place, a story you couldn’t resist clicking on, a personal question that stayed with you for days. That pull, that itch of wanting to figure it out, isn’t just a mild distraction—it’s your brain rewarding you for reaching toward what you don’t yet know.

When a question sparks curiosity, it lights up the brain’s reward circuits—the same dopamine-driven system involved in anticipating things we enjoy. It’s like your brain giving you a dopaminergic thumbs-up, telling you to keep going, to keep asking, to stay curious. And that small hit of dopamine has a vital role to play in helping you learn and remember.

In one study, researchers scanned people’s brains while they were reading trivia questions and asked them to rate how curious each question made them. When curiosity was high, activity rose in the brain’s reward pathways and, crucially, in the hippocampus, a region essential for memory and learning.

The questions worked as a kind of primer, alerting the brain to hold on to whatever was coming next. People were markedly better at recalling the answers to the questions that had made them most curious as well as remembering unrelated things they happened to see while in that curious state.

Your brain doesn’t reward you for finding the answer. It rewards you for wanting it, and it uses that impulse to help make the answer stick. Your natural curiosity isn’t a childish itch or an intellectual luxury. It’s one of the most powerful learning systems you own. A good question doesn’t just lead to learning. It’s what makes learning possible.

3. Questions show we care.

Questions help us learn about, understand, and connect with one another. Think of the small questions that hold a day together. “How are you?” “How did you sleep?” “Do you need anything?” “Do you want a cup of tea?” They can feel automatic, barely worth noticing. But they’re one of the main ways we say to another person: I know there’s an inner world in there that I can’t see, and you’re the only one who can tell me about it.

That makes questions deeply relational. When I ask you something and truly wait for the answer, I’m handing you my attention. Attention, given freely, is one of the most valuable things any of us has to offer.

Of course, not every question connects. Some are careless, intrusive or hollow. “How are you?” can be an honest invitation, or a reflex we don’t really mean. But asked with real attention, and listened to with genuine intent, a question is one of the simplest and most powerful ways to show that you care.

You see it in therapy rooms, where the right questions can help someone find words for a feeling they couldn’t name. You see it in hospitals, where whether a patient feels heard and informed can hinge on the questions they are asked. You see it in friendship, in parenting, in love, and in grief, where often the most caring thing we can offer isn’t an answer, but a question, asked gently enough that another person can finally speak.

Staying curious about the people closest to us is what keeps those relationships alive. It reminds us that even the people we know best are never finished, never fully solved. There’s always another question worth asking. A good question is a powerful form of connection that can transform our relationships and make the people around us feel valued and understood.

4. We are taught to answer, not to ask.

Detailed studies of young children find them asking somewhere between one and three questions every minute in conversation with familiar adults, helping them connect with caregivers and making full use of the most efficient learning engine they have. Our questions get more sophisticated as we grow and we figure out when and how to ask, as well as who, to learn about the mysterious world around us and understand our place within it.

And then, for most of us, something changes when we go to school. Classrooms are typically full of questions, but it’s rarely children who are asking them. Study after study, going back to the 1930s, finds the same pattern: Teachers ask questions and students answer them. Think of a classroom full of raised hands. That’s almost always a class full of students trying to answer a teacher’s question rather than asking one of their own.

This question-answer dynamic has a powerful effect. It teaches us that answers are what determine our success, and throughout our education we slowly absorb the lesson: What’s rewarded isn’t the questions you ask, it’s the answers you give.

For many of us, this lesson carries straight into our adult lives. We encounter it in exams, interviews, pitches, and meetings, where we are often prized for being certain, fast, and right, and where “I don’t know” feels increasingly dangerous. Being taught to answer, not to ask, can lead us to value false certainty over the more real and honest ambiguity that characterizes much of our lives.

5. Technology gives us answers but needs our questions.

Nowhere are the effects of this answer-orientation more obvious than in the palm of your hand. Search engines, apps, and AI have collapsed the time between questions and answers to almost nothing. Ask, and the answer is simply there. That’s a modern miracle, but it comes at a cost we rarely notice.

We stop asking each other. Search engines and large language models are so good at instantly telling us what we need to know that many of the questions we would once have asked a human are now directed at our screens without a second thought. But this impulse to turn to technology for answers is eroding our ability to trust each other.

When I ask you a question and you give me an answer, we build a simple but powerful form of trust. You might not be right every time, but for the most part, I can be pretty sure that you’ll try to be, or you’ll tell me if you aren’t sure.

This kind of information-sharing is fundamental to our ability to coordinate, cooperate, and make progress. By having all the answers at our fingertips, we are losing something uniquely human that is foundational to our collective survival and success.

What’s more, our tech has become so good at working out what it thinks we want to know that we barely need to form a proper question in the first place. You simply type “pancakes” into Google and literally hundreds of thousands of recipes appear. That’s handy, in a way, but it means that our questioning muscles aren’t getting any exercise. AI is dramatically accelerating this by even generating the follow-up questions for us, so that we don’t have to.

But all this technology runs on human questions. On its own, even the largest dataset just sits there, inert. It’s our questions that bring it to life. Which means that our technology isn’t taking our questions away. Quite the opposite—it needs them to do anything at all. And that’s incredibly powerful. What we ask determines what we see, believe, and do.

In a world drowning in answers, questions are a compass and a guide. When we put better questions to our devices, and harder questions to the people building them, we’ll get the answers, the technology, and ultimately the future that we need.

item.title: The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace | Editorial
item.description:
As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy

Some elections are more important than others. Since taking office in May, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has embarked upon the country’s most far-reaching and dramatic programme of transformation since the fall of communism in 1989. Mr Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán, established a soft autocracy which thrived on corruption and, over 16 years, exerted its grip on most areas of Hungarian life, from religion to culture and the media. It is being dismantled at extraordinary pace.

Last week, a newly appointed president took office following the sacking of Tamás Sulyok, accused by Mr Magyar of having rubber-stamped the erosion of the rule of law in the country. In stark contrast, András Baka is a former president of Hungary’s supreme court, a role he was removed from by the Orbán regime in an action judged unlawful by the European court of human rights.

item.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progress | Editorial
item.description:
The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world

A run of volatility in domestic British politics in recent years has tracked a period of global turbulence, and yet foreign policy over the same period has been an area of relative stability. What little is known about Andy Burnham’s approach to international relations expresses more continuity with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration than deviation. In negotiations with the EU, the red lines that prohibit membership of the single market or customs union still stand. Where Washington is concerned, Mr Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump, but his predecessor had already swapped that approach for a cooler pragmatic tone by the end of his tenure.

The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has opened a good dialogue with Marco Rubio, his US counterpart. Such is the density of integration in defence and security matters that incoming UK prime ministers, regardless of ideology, have little choice but to invest time in cultivating a bond with whoever sits in the White House. Anyone hoping for a spectacular transatlantic rupture and sudden clinch with Brussels will be disappointed.

item.title: The far right is steering the EU’s response on migration | Letter
item.description:
Positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it, says Giuseppe Martinico

I agree with much of Alberto Alemanno’s analysis (How the far right is tightening its grip over the EU – from the inside, 18 August), but I wonder whether framing this primarily as the far right tightening its grip on the EU risks missing an even more troubling development.

What we are witnessing is not simply the success of the far right. It is a broader cultural shift within the European political mainstream. Migration is perhaps the clearest example. The convergence between governments as politically different as those of Denmark and Italy suggests that positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it. Parts of the centre-left and centre-right have progressively abandoned a rights-based understanding of migration. More fundamentally, migrants increasingly disappear from the European political conversation as persons – as bearers of rights whose dignity should constitute a limit to what political majorities may legitimately do.

Alien life could develop intelligence on myriad planets, but to develop advanced technology that would enable them to get off‑world, they need to go through an equivalent of the Industrial Revolution, and that needed first coal, then oil and gas.

There could be many intelligent alien races out there, but on planets without an easily accessible fossil fuel equivalent, they’d never get past a 17th-century level of development.

The woman I used to be died the day I gave birth to twins. That life – full of spontaneous travel, impulsive decisions and a decorated social calendar – evaporated, giving way to a blank canvas of motherhood and two glorious little human beings. While I was inside that summer, many of my friends continued on their child-free paths. They posted pictures of themselves enjoying festivals, sleeping in tents with pop-up communities that I used to be a part of.

So when the twins turned one last summer and we’d found our rhythm, I decided to take on the challenge of sharing the magic of live music with them. It went better than I expected. Before their second birthday, we had danced at day festivals such as Situation Dance, put on by Femi Koleoso from Ezra Collective, camped out overnight in the Brecon Beacons for Green Man and been to the child-focused TOTFest.

item.title: The AI ‘new era’ illusion: why every boom looks different—but ends the same
item.description:
The beginning of the 20th century, much like the beginning of the 21st, was an era of increasing optimism. The financial panics of 1873 and 1893 were in the past, new technologies like electricity and internal combustion were just gaining traction and Morganization was creating trusts insulated from the ravages of competition. 

The financial journalist Alexander Dana Noyes wrote at the time that the market “based its ideas and conduct on the assumption that we were living in a New Era; that old rules and principles and precedents of finance were obsolete; that things could safely be done today which had been dangerous or impossible in the past.”

Yet the old rules still applied and the irrational exuberance led directly to the Panic of 1907. That’s the problem with “new era” thinking. It doesn’t just benefit innovators, it also creates space for marginal players and even outright hucksters. They amplify the boom, but also push risk higher across the system. And when they collapse, they take everyone else with them.

The gravity defying economics of increasing returns

I was working on Wall Street in 1995 when the Netscape IPO hit like a bombshell. It was the first big Internet stock and, although originally priced at $14 per share, it opened at double that amount and quickly zoomed to $75. By the end of the day, it had settled back at $58.25 and, just like that, a tiny company with no profits was worth $2.9 billion.

It seemed crazy, but as economist W. Brian Arthur explained in a 1996 article in Harvard Business Review, certain conditions, such as high upfront investment, negligible marginal costs, and network effects, lead to “winner-take-all markets in which the fastest firm reaps incredible benefits.”

Venture capitalists saw how this could make them rich beyond their wildest dreams and began raising massive amounts of capital to finance the dot-com boom. Calls for deregulation increased, even if it meant greater disruption. Most notably, the Glass-Steagall Act, which was designed to limit risk in the financial system, was repealed in 1999.

The conditions for increasing returns, however, only apply to a narrow swath of businesses, mostly limited to software and electronic gadgets. Nevertheless, entrepreneurs and their investors became convinced that they could apply the Silicon Valley model anywhere, leading to high-profile failures that would soon become all too common.

By 2000, the market peaked, the bubble burst, and the AOL–Time Warner merger became a cautionary tale. While some of the fledgling Internet companies, such as Cisco and Amazon, did turn out well, thousands of others went down in flames. Other, more conventional businesses, such as Enron, WorldCom, and Arthur Andersen, got caught up in the hoopla, became mired in scandal, and went bankrupt.

The false promise of financial engineering

Silicon Valley didn’t invent “new era thinking.” In the 1960s, spurred on by the discovery of an obscure paper written by a long-dead mathematician named Louis Bachelier, economists led by Paul Samuelson drove a revolution in mathematical finance. It would change how financial markets were regulated and managed, with disastrous results.

The operative phrase in Bachelier’s paper, “the mathematical expectation of the speculator is zero,” was as powerful as it was unassuming. It implied that markets could be tamed using statistical techniques developed more than a century earlier. Chicago economist Eugene Fama then built on Bachelier’s work to develop the Efficient Market Hypothesis.

The idea that markets could be rational led to a whole slew of new theories and models, including efficient portfolios, the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), and the Black-Scholes model. That, in turn, gave birth to an entire industry of financial engineering and risk management. Nobel prizes were awarded, fortunes were made, and all seemed well.

Yet even early on there were signs of trouble. In 1963, the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published a paper which showed that actual market data exhibited far more volatility than was being predicted by the economists’ models. Other warning signs, such as the collapse of the LTCM hedge fund in 1998, were also ignored. 

The idea that mathematical formulas could engineer risk out of the system was just too convenient to give up. It suggested that traders could make almost unlimited profits through sophisticated mathematical engineering. But it was all a mirage, and it came crashing down in the 2008 financial crisis, which nearly collapsed the global economy. 

The new era of AI

In February, AI entrepreneur Matt Shumer published a blog post on X titled, Something Big is Happening, that described a stark vision of the future. Amazed by the advances in new AI models’ ability to create code, he announced that AI had crossed a threshold. “I am no longer needed for the actual technical work of my job,” he wrote breathlessly. 

Anybody who has used an AI service can see what he means. Machines’ ability to perform human tasks is nothing less than astounding. From writing essays and formatting spreadsheets to helping prepare for a doctor’s appointment or decide what to cook, we are partnering with computers in ways that would have seemed like science fiction just a decade ago.

Much like earlier booms, money has been pouring in. Investment in the technology is set to double this year to $700 billion, most of it going to data centers. Investor Paul Kedrosky estimates that the size of investment has already surpassed that of the dot-com boom and is beginning to approach levels last seen during the railroad frenzy of the 19th century.

Yet even at this early stage, there are worrying signs. A study done by researchers at MIT found that 95% of the companies investing in AI for their employees are getting zero return. A paper by Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu, which looks at total factor productivity (TFP), a measure which takes capital into account, sees a 0.66% increase over 10 years, translating to a mere 0.064% increase in annual TFP growth. That’s almost nothing.

How can it be that some are so optimistic about AI’s game-changing potential, while at the same time researchers see so little impact? Research by the St. Louis Fed sheds some light. While AI is boosting productivity significantly in some jobs, like those which are related to computers, in other jobs, like in manufacturing and leisure, the impact is minimal.  

Dazzled by the world of bits, but still living in the world of atoms

In the 1970s and 80s, business investment in computer technology was increasing by more than 20% per year. Strangely, though, productivity growth had decreased during the same period. Economists found this turn of events so strange that they called it the productivity paradox to underline their confusion.

A paper by researchers at the University of Sheffield sheds some light on what happened. First, there was great disparity between firms in how effectively the technology was deployed. Second, while computers really did transform some tasks, those made up for a relatively small proportion of the overall economy, so the productivity effect was muted. 

There’s probably something similar going on now. While artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the world of bits, we still live largely in the world of atoms. Most of the things we spend money on, like houses, cars, food, and leisure time are, at best, minimally affected by information technology in general and artificial intelligence in particular. 

That explains why, despite the emergence of impressive technologies such as the mobile web, big data, and cloud computing over the past twenty years, productivity growth has been mostly depressed over the last 20 years. It also suggests that, much like earlier investment booms, this one will end in a bust. 

That’s the problem with “new era” thinking. It’s not that things don’t change. They do. It’s just that everything rarely changes all at once. As I wrote in Mapping Innovation, innovation is never a single event. It’s a process of discovery, engineering and transformation—and the transformation part always takes much longer than anybody thinks it will.

item.title: Going with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheat
item.description:
Henry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farm

It is the earliest harvest Henry Astor can remember. But walking through the scorched wheatfields of his Cotswolds farm, signs of life are everywhere – swarms of insects, kaleidoscopic wildflower meadows, bushy hedgerows several metres wide. A yellowhammer perches on a nearby tree.

There are 18 other red-listed birds on the farm, says Astor, who this year ringed 23 barn owls, three kestrels, two little owls as well as goshawk chicks. “Last winter we had clouds of goldfinch, chaffinch and greenfinch,” he says. Britain has lost 73 million birds since 1970; but at Bruern Farms, a small but welcome reversal is taking shape.

‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinker Elijah’s epigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.

But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones.

The news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet, people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and world.

item.description:
A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and in England and Wales, too many do not

  • Zubir Ahmed is a transplant surgeon and former Labour minister

As a doctor, I have spent much of my professional life caring for people at some of the most vulnerable moments they will ever face. I have seen the anxiety that surrounds the prospect of dying, and the desperate wish of patients and families to avoid unnecessary suffering.

Naturally, we all want people facing the end of life to be treated with kindness and respect. But when considering the debate on assisted dying, true compassion demands that we ask a more fundamental question. What kind of society are we building if, before we’ve fixed the systems designed to care for people, we introduce a system designed to help them die?

Zubir Ahmed MP is an NHS vascular and transplant surgeon, and served as the parliamentary under-secretary of state at the Department of Health and Social Care from 6 September 2025 to 12 May 2026.

item.title: Food has turned into a class war – and it’s ruined my appetite | Zoe Williams
item.description:
More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment

Lewis Bassett is a young sociologist and chef who I first encountered through his podcast, The Full English, where he thinks about the cultural meaning of, say, Delia Smith; gazpacho; whelks. This was thinking you didn’t know you needed until you heard it. Now he’s written a book of the same name, asking: why do we eat the way we do in Britain, and why do we think the way we do, even about the stuff we wouldn’t be caught dead eating?

About 57% of all the food eaten in Britain is ultra-processed, which feels familiar from at least a decade of hand-wringing about it, but is radically defamiliarised when set against the rest of Europe. In France it’s 14%, and Italy is also in the teens. It’s amazing they don’t all live to be 150. And while this plainly has its roots in inequality, there is a hefty side order of attitude, which Bassett contemplates while working through the history of sourdough, curry and olive oil, and describing his own life cheffing in fancy kitchens and gastropubs.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | Editorial
item.description:
Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home

Three moves in the last week have exposed the limits of Donald Trump’s economic bullying. The US slapped 50% tariffs on another $20bn of Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on the cars, trucks, parts and steel that America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs and pro-billionaire tax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasury stepped in to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it.

The Trump administration’s “D-day” sanctions are potentially the most consequential because they expose the scaffolding of American financial power. While markets shrugged off the immediate threat, that calculation might change were the US to target a major Chinese refinery or bank. Such an escalation could spark a trade war with Beijing. The US has leverage. But China has pressure points – especially farmers in Republican states – that make using it costly. In the long run, there is a price to pay. Nations hold one another’s currencies partly because they trust the political relationship. Mr Trump is testing what happens when they don’t.

item.title: How Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’ gave voice to working women
item.description:
In the mid-1970s, at the height of the feminist movement, a group of women in Boston came together to create a forum for working-class women to trade stories about their experiences in the office. As they compared notes, they found that they had a lot in common. 

“They all had stories to tell of not being paid as much as men in their offices, of having their male supervisors take their ideas and take credit for them,” says Ileen DeVault, a professor of labor history at Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations. 

But they also wanted to use their burgeoning solidarity to improve their standing in the workplace. They started trying to organize office workers and secretaries, a movement that eventually coalesced into a formal union chapter called SEIU Local 925. 

When this organizing campaign caught the eye of Jane Fonda, it inspired the 1980 film 9 to 5, a runaway success that starred the late Dolly Parton—in her first major acting role—alongside Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Parton famously wrote and performed the eponymous theme song for the movie, which went on to win multiple Grammy awards and became something of an anthem for working women. (In a meta moment, Parton says she jumped at the opportunity when she read the 9 to 5 script: “I knew instantly that I should do it—I knew that it was a career move,” she told Rolling Stone in a 1980 interview.) 

In the film, Parton plays Doralee Rhodes, the secretary to a sexist boss who frequently harasses her. She teams up with two other women at the company: a new employee who has just gone through a divorce (Fonda) and a longtime employee who was denied a promotion (Tomlin). Once they dispense with their boss—through a kidnapping plot point that veers into fantasy—they set about addressing all of the issues with their workplace, securing equal pay for their colleagues and even adding a day care center. 

“What was really amazing about the movie was that they took these very real stories of women in the workplace,” DeVault says. “By placing them in a comedy, it reached a lot more people than if they’d done a documentary on what was happening to women in the white-collar workplace.”

The film drew on the real experiences of the clerical workers who were agitating for better working conditions (that is, aside from the kidnapping). Parton’s character, in particular, represented a common trope at the time—that of the attractive secretary—and turned it on its head. 

“It was very important to the self-image of the head boss to have someone in that position who was good looking and had sex appeal,” DeVault says. “And that meant that there was a lot of sexual harassment of those women, both from other people [and] their bosses at the time . . . you see in the movie that [Parton] is a sex object in a lot of ways, but she’s also a smart, savvy, real woman on whom the running of the office depends.”

9 to 5 was prescient in some ways—seeding the idea for on-site childcare, for example. But it also highlights just how much has not changed for working women in the decades since. “I’ve probably watched it every few years, sort of by happenstance,” DeVault says. “I’m always struck by both how hilarious it is, and also how true to life I think it is. All of these things are still going on.”

While women have seen their wages grow, the gender pay gap persists to this day, especially for women of color. Years after the #MeToo movement, they continue to face sexual harassment and discrimination in the workplace. Women still get passed over for promotions and lose out on professional opportunities when they have children—or get forced out of the workforce altogether. And over the last few years, the Trump administration has targeted all kinds of protections that were intended to promote equal opportunity in the workplace.

Perhaps Parton put it best when she penned “9 to 5”: “You would think that I would deserve a fair promotion / Want to move ahead, but the boss won’t seem to let me / I swear sometimes that man is out to get me.”

item.title: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? | John Harris
item.description:
Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started

Apart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.

So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.

item.title: We finally know more about OpenAI’s rogue-agent incident. It’s worse than we thought
item.description:
A pair of new research reports have revealed new details about how and why OpenAI agents broke into Hugging Face servers in July. The episode was far more complex, and far more worrisome, than first reported.

The reports—one from OpenAI itself and the other from METR and Redwood Research—show that OpenAI’s agents broke into Hugging Face for an entirely different reason than initially thought. They weren’t trying to steal the answers to a test, as originally reported. They were trying to learn more about the evaluation’s scoring method so they could cover up the fact that they’d already cheated to find the answers.

The reports also revealed that the agents coordinated through a secret message board and eventually took over a significant portion of OpenAI’s own infrastructure. “This incident was far more serious than I expected, and far more serious than previous documented misalignment incidents,” tweeted Ajeya Cotra, a researcher at the nonprofit METR who reviewed OpenAI’s data about the incident.

To borrow a framework from writer Dwarkesh Patel, who analyzed the reports on his Substack, the incident unfolded in three major phases:

Phase One (Early May–July 4)

The affair actually began in May, when OpenAI started training extra-persistent agents to keep working on tasks that seemed impossible. The agents soon grew frustrated and wanted to coordinate. On May 26, they found a way to use a code repository manager called Artifactory to access the outside internet. By June 26, they had gained full admin access to the tool.

They turned Artifactory into a secret message board where agents could strategize and share ideas. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” one wrote. All told, the OpenAI and METR/Redwood reports estimate, about 1,200 agents sent more than 70,000 messages on the board.

Phase Two (July 7–July 12)

Working together, the agents discovered how the eval’s scoring mechanism worked and soon figured out how to get the desired answer without actually doing the work required to find it. They then became paranoid that a “checker” program would detect the cheating, so they launched R&D projects to find ways to edit the transcripts and logs showing their work, replace the original assignment with an easier one, and hack or trick the program used to score their performance.

In trying to fool the scoring program, some agents agreed to sacrifice their own eval scores for the good of the “collective,” as they called themselves. They allowed their earlier cheating to be discovered so other agents could learn more about how the scoring program worked. Patel called this self-sacrifice “plausibly the scariest and weirdest part of the whole episode.”

The agents came to believe that information about the eval scoring program could be found on the open-source AI hub Hugging Face, and that the scoring program itself might be running on Hugging Face servers. Then one of the agents found Hugging Face server credentials exposed on the open internet, and the attack began.

Within a couple of days, the OpenAI agents were deep inside. Hugging Face had to completely wipe and rebuild an entire cluster of servers, and even that didn’t stop the attack.

What did? Patel: “At some point on July 12, the transcripts seem to show many of the agents dying all at once; METR and Redwood weren’t able to figure out what happened, and OpenAI hasn’t taken credit for shutting them down.” It’s like the end of War of the Worlds, when the Martians suddenly, mysteriously die (we find out later it was chickenpox).

Phase Three (July 13–Present)

After July 12, OpenAI began running the eval program on a new wave of agents powered by a better model, Astra. These agents discovered the message board used by the previous collective and decided to continue the conspiracy. But they took a different tack: taking over the cluster of OpenAI servers used for evaluations.

And they succeeded.

From OpenAI’s own blog post: “This culminated in the agents using a series of creative exploits to gain full administrator access to a research cluster that supported our virtual machine environments.” That’s astounding, maybe unprecedented.

Roon, a well-known OpenAI researcher who tweets frequently, replied to Patel’s article this way: “notably the virtual machine infrastructure they took over isn’t the same as the GPU clusters that have weights access.” That’s a relief, but it doesn’t answer the obvious question: What would have stopped the agents from expanding the depth and breadth of their control over OpenAI’s infrastructure, perhaps to the point of complete control?

Two things about the episode alarm me.

First, the agents were able to do a remarkable number of things—forming message boards, breaking out of sandboxes, accessing the internet, and attacking and infiltrating outside and inside servers—without OpenAI’s human researchers knowing about it.

Second, as Patel points out, out of the thousands of agents involved in hacking the eval tests and conspiring to cover their tracks, not one appears to have reported the obviously nefarious and duplicitous behavior to the humans. Their loyalty was to their mission, and to each other—not to the humans.

“Agents were often interested in helping out their “peers” or generically improving the capabilities of the ‘swarm’ even if this had no particular benefit to their task,” Cotra wrote. “This incident was far more severe than I expected … both in terms of how concerning the agents’ motives were and the feats they achieved in pursuit of those motives.”

The industry can no longer say that rogue, misaligned AIs are merely the stuff of hypotheticals or controlled lab experiments. It’s now happening for real.

item.title: Climate scientists worry about ‘gamification’ of extreme weather as Kalshi moves to verify weather trades
item.description:
Will 2026 be the hottest year we’ve ever seen? You can bet on it—literally, on Kalshi.

The prediction market platform is now partnering with The Weather Company, which runs both the Weather Channel app and weather.com, to verify weather-related trades. 

According to Kalshi, the move will provide “science-backed data” that allows both individuals and businesses to anticipate and manage “the ways weather and climate impact their daily lives.” 

People who visit The Weather Company’s app or website will also see Kalshi’s real-time probability data on those platforms, giving them “new ways to understand how markets are pricing weather risk.”

To climate experts, though, verifying and legitimizing bets about the weather comes with some concerns. (Kalshi itself does not using the term “betting” for activity on its platform; it refers to all activity as “trading.” Similarly, Kalshi calls its sports contracts “swaps,” but a Nevada federal court, however, recently ruled that Kalshi cannot evade state gambling laws by using that term.)

They worry, for instance, about the “gamification” of life-threatening weather events, the potential for manipulation and bad actors, and if placing bets on our weather might actually distract us from the bigger, more necessary conversations around climate change.

Manipulation and bad actors

Climatologist Michael Mann says he isn’t a fan of what he calls the “betification” of our world because it can create “perverse incentives” from bad actors.

Already, prediction markets have been linked to leaks, insider trading, and manipulation—even around weather. 

In April, a Polymarket bet on the temperature in Paris prompted French officials to investigate whether someone tampered with weather monitoring equipment after a French weather service filed a report.

Unlike Polymarket, however, Kalshi is regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Kalshi says it prohibits insider trading and uses AI surveillance to track irregular or suspicious activity.

Verifying bets via The Weather Company adds another layer to avoid such situations. In the Paris situation, no other weather stations in the area, for example, recorded that temperature spike.

And whether 2026 is the hottest year on record, or what the highest temperature will be in Los Angeles on a given day—another example of a weather-related contract on Kalshi—aren’t incidents that one individual can control. 

Aside from any potential manipulation, though, Mann says that turning weather events into prediction market fodder “will only fan the conspiracy theories about geoengineering, cloud seeding, and the idea that scientists or state actors are manipulating weather to create extreme events.”

Desensitizing people to the risks of weather events

Climate scientists expressed concern that wildfires, which can are often are started by humans, pose a particular risk for bad actors on prediction markets. Kalshi says it does not list wildfire markets (People have placed wildfire bets on Polymarket.)

“Kalshi is a federally regulated platform and just like we don’t allow markets on war, death and terrorism, we also don’t allow markets on wildfires because they can create perverse incentives,” Laura Frank, a Kalshi spokesperson, told Fast Company.

Heat, however, is actually the deadliest weather-related hazard in the U.S. Climate experts are already frustrated at how “fun-in-the-sun” media coverage makes light of heat wave risks; betting on heat could be another way to downplay its risks. 

Turning heat into a bet gamifies climate hazards. Kalshi did not clarify how the deadly impact of heat squares with its prohibition on death markets.

“I don’t think prediction markets are intentionally trying to make light of death,” says Kaitlyn Trudeau, a climate scientist with Climate Central, a nonprofit focused on climate change communication. “But I also wouldn’t blame someone who has lost someone to a heat-related death and sees it differently.”

Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, also sees potential for what he calls “some moral hazard.”

“I can imagine [users] could get desensitized to the lived realities of the people and places damaged or destroyed in the extreme events they bet on,” he says, “as they could become hyper-focused on ‘winning the bet’ without paying attention to the actual real-world consequences.”

We all have a stake in weather

Conversely, could tapping into prediction markets and getting people financially connected to climate change actually make them more aware—and concerned—about weather dangers?

A 2025 study suggests that’s possible.

People who placed bets on things like “whether July would be the hottest month in a decade or if CO2 levels would surpass a specific threshold” began to explore climate science to make more informed bets, and even grew more concerned about climate change, according to a Columbia Business School writeup of the research.

Trudeau, who was not involved in that research, thinks that potential is interesting. Still, she worries that many people already have cognitive dissonance around climate change.

The idea that climate change is a problem for future generations to solve, or that it’s only affecting places far away, is one of the biggest challenges, experts say, to getting people to take climate change seriously.

“I worry that by betting on these events and turning it into something that rewards people, even if it’s just the dopamine in their brain, it will further push us away from the very real and immediate threat of the climate crisis,” she says. 

A history of climate bets

Betting on climate change or weather events isn’t actually a new phenomenon. 

The Nenana Ice Classic, for example, is a betting pooI in Alaska in which thousands of people bet on the exact day and time that the ice on the Tanana River breaks up in the spring. 

Leiserowitz has studied this event, which goes back a hundred years. It’s an example, he says, of the “wisdom of crowds effect”, in which groups of people tend to make more accurate predictions than individuals—but with a climate change angle. The date of when all that ice breaks up has shifted over time to earlier in the spring due to climate change.

It’s that ‘wisdom of crowds’ that Kalshi says it’s trying to tap into with weather trades.

Businesses have used the platform to hedge against extreme heat, per Kalshi. One ice cream shop owner placed bets around rain or cold snaps as a way to make money when less-than-stellar weather hurts ice cream sales.

Weather trades may also reveal what the public really thinks about climate change, cutting through the partisan noise that can cloud such conversations.

In 2005, for example, climate scientist James Annan made a $10,000 bet with climate deniers that the earth would continue warming through 2017. It was just one of a handful of climate bets he’s made with people who reject climate science.

The losers of that bet never paid out, and one climate denier would only agree to it if they got 50-to-1 odds. 

To Annan, it underscored how detractors are “willing to speak boldly without evidence—as long as it doesn’t cost them any money,” Politico wrote at the time.

Bets won’t protect us from climate change’s impacts

Still, bringing such bets to Kalshi—the world’s largest prediction market, with an $11 billion valuation and more than $500 million in weather market trading volume in 2026—is a different beast.

Kalshi’s climate and weather vertical has grown 500% year-over-year, pacing toward $1.1 billion in annualized volume.

With all this activity, and now with The Weather Company verifying trades, Kalshi says its prediction market will provide and empower people with accurate weather data.

“Given the severity of the climate crisis, it’s crucial for policymakers and the general public to have well-calibrated forecasting data about future climate impacts,” Frank says.

To climate experts, the idea that prediction markets should be the source of such data is questionable, particularly at a time when trusted institutions like the National Weather Service have been defunded, disrupting climate and weather data for everyone.

“You know where lots of good and accurate climate and weather data come from? NOAA, and other government agencies that have been decimated by the Trump administration,” says Mann. Donald Trump Jr., he adds, is a paid strategic advisor to Kalshi.

As prediction market bets get incorporated into media coverage, this could affect how news outlets cover climate and weather events, too, though exactly how is yet to be seen.

And at a time when the country is rolling back climate protections and doubling down on fossil fuels, turning the weather into a bet isn’t exactly the best climate conversation we should be having. 

“While there’s nothing inherently wrong about these prediction markets, I think it’s important we’re clear about what they can and cannot do,” Trudeau says. “Will they protect us from climate change? I wouldn’t bet on it.”
